stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Pick a material from the palette and drop it into the sample slot. Move the length slider. Watch how the current $I$ and the category bar respond.
stages.concept: The resistance of a sample of length $\ell$ and cross-section $S$ is $R = \rho \cdot \ell / S$, where $\rho$ is the material's resistivity. Low $\rho$ (metals) $\Rightarrow$ high current $\Rightarrow$ conductor. Very high $\rho$ (plastic, dry wood) $\Rightarrow$ almost no current $\Rightarrow$ insulator.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Hit each target lamp state. Choose a material and a length so the lamp reaches the requested brightness.
stages.concept: The lamp lights brightly for good conductors, glows dimly for materials of intermediate resistivity (semi-conductors like graphite), and stays off for insulators. Geometry matters: doubling the length doubles $R$ and halves $I$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The current readout is hidden. From the material and geometry shown, predict the lamp state: bright, dim, or off. Three correct predictions in a row.
stages.concept: Categorise materials by orders of magnitude of $\rho$. Metals: $\rho \approx 10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. Graphite: $\rho \approx 10^{-4}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. Salt water: $\rho \approx 10^{-1}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$. Pure water and plastic: $\rho \geq 10^{5}\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$.

labels.tip1: pick materials one by one; slide length to see it stretch and thin the current
labels.tip2: graphite lights the lamp dimly when long; a metal wire always burns bright
labels.tip3: one attempt per scenario — reason before you click
labels.peek_tip: R = ρ·ℓ/S. Larger ρ or longer sample ⇒ higher R ⇒ smaller I. Rank the material's ρ before answering.

1.1: Drop any material into the slot on the right side of the loop.
1.2: Try a metal first, then a plastic. The lamp brightness should be very different.
1.3: Now try graphite and drag the length slider. That is the interesting middle case.

2.1: For BRIGHT: any metal works. Copper or aluminum at any length.
2.2: For DIM: graphite with a long length. The formula R = ρ·ℓ/S grows R when ℓ grows.
2.3: For OFF: pick a poor conductor — tap water, distilled water, or plastic. Length barely matters.

3.1: Look at ρ. If it's around 10⁻⁸ the material is a metal — bright.
3.2: Compute R = ρ·ℓ/S in your head (S = 10⁻⁶ m²). Then I ≈ 12 / (100 + R).
3.3: Bright if I > 60 mA. Dim if I between 3 and 60 mA. Off if I < 3 mA.
